s: Large language model, Large Language Model (LLM); the GPT series behind ChatGPT is this kind of model.
Reads in some text and keeps writing it, one char at a time; answering, writing, translating and coding all rest on this one skill.

• Five training steps: mass text → token dictionary → pre-training → fine-tuning → alignment
  • Model parameters: what training produces: a huge pile of numbers
  • Five use steps: text comes in → tokenize → the Transformer computes with the parameters → pick the next char → append and go again

1. Training: practise “guess the next char” on mass text, then adjust with Q&A examples and human ratings; the parameters are fixed
  2. Use: “天空是什么颜色？” (What colour is the sky?) → tokenize → compute by reading the parameters
  3. this site’s small model gives “蓝” (blue) 99.8% this site’s real model → pick “蓝”, append it → compute the next char, until the end

ProblemBefore, every task (translation, classification, Q&A…) needed its own human-labelled data and its own separately trained model.
Research · findingGPT (Radford et al., 2018) first pre-trained on lots of unlabelled text, then fine-tuned per task, and beat the purpose-built models of the time on most test tasks; GPT-2 (2019) found that a bigger model could do some tasks without fine-tuning; GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020, 175 billion parameters) could do a new task from just a few examples in the prompt.
DesignTurn every task into one thing — guess the next char; pre-train on mass text first, then fine-tune and align so it answers well and more reliably.
Why it worksTo guess the next char well it must learn grammar, common sense and some reasoning; and the bigger the model, data and compute, the more regularly the error falls (see the “Scaling laws” card).
Pre-training corpus and data cleaning (Data Cleaning / Filtering).
Prepares the material the model learns from: large in amount, varied in kind, good in quality.

• Sources: web pages (e.g. the public web-crawl archive Common Crawl), books, encyclopaedias, papers, code, dialogue
  • De-duplication: delete repeated text
  • Quality filtering: delete garbled text, ads, template pages, too-short fragments
  • Safety filtering: remove harmful content and personal private data
  • Mix: how much of each source to use

1. 3 sentences crawled: “天空是蓝色的。” “天空是蓝色的。” “点击领红包!!!” (an ad) example number
  2. De-duplication deletes sentence 2, quality filtering deletes sentence 3; 1 sentence is left
  3. GPT-3’s data: filtered Common Crawl, WebText2, two book corpora and English Wikipedia; about 300 billion tokens were used in training

ProblemRaw web pages are full of repeats, ads, garbled text and errors; the model takes it all in: “garbage in, garbage out”.
Research · findingGPT-2 (2019) did not use the whole web: it only took pages linked from Reddit posts with at least 3 upvotes (WebText), using human picks as a quality signal; GPT-3 (2020) sampled higher-quality sources more often in training; Lee et al. (2021) found that after de-duplication the model recited training text word for word much less (roughly).
DesignMix many sources + de-duplicate + quality and safety filters + set the mix by quality.
Why it worksWhat the model learns is the patterns in the data: the cleaner and more varied the data, the more reliable the patterns, and the less garbage it memorises.

KC03.no: Built in training, looked up in use
s: Token dictionary / vocabulary (Vocabulary); a common algorithm is BPE (byte-pair encoding); tokenizing in detail: layer 4, the “Tokenization” card.
Fixes a “text ↔ number” table before training starts; training and use both look up this same book.

• Entries: one number per token
  • Merge rules: the order in which pairs are merged
  • Special symbols: e.g. “end”, “chat role”
  • Size: e.g. GPT-2 has about 50 thousand (50257)

1. First split the text into the smallest units (chars or bytes)
  2. Count which two pieces sit together most often (e.g. “蓝” “色”), merge them into “蓝色” and add it; repeat until big enough
  3. “天空是蓝色的” → 天空 | 是 | 蓝色 | 的 → 812 15 3301 9 example number

ProblemA dictionary of whole words: far too many words, and new words are unknown; single letters or bytes: sentences get too long and slow to compute.
Research · findingBPE was a data-compression method by Gage (1994); Sennrich et al. (2016) used it for machine translation and found a limited dictionary can spell any word, with rare words split into common pieces.
DesignFrequent pieces are stored whole, rare ones split smaller; from GPT-2 on, “byte-level BPE” can encode any text.
Why it worksIt balances dictionary size against sentence length. Training and use must share one book: the rows of the embedding table and the columns of the output table follow the numbers, so a new dictionary matches nothing.
Pre-training, a kind of self-supervised learning; the task is next-token prediction, also called causal language modelling.
Lets the model practise “guess the next char” on mass text by itself, storing language patterns and knowledge in the parameters.

• Training text: cut into fixed-length pieces
  • Transformer: parameters start as random numbers
  • Loss: cross-entropy, how wrong the guess is (see layer 4, the “Loss function: cross-entropy” card)
  • Backprop + optimiser: (often Adam): works out and makes each parameter’s change
  • Lots of GPUs: compute in parallel

1. “天空是蓝色的” is 5 questions at once: 天→空, 天空→是, 天空是→蓝, 天空是蓝→色, 天空是蓝色→的
  2. The causal mask lets each position see only what is before it, so all 5 are practised in one pass
  3. This site’s small model: at first p(蓝) = 5.4%, a big error → change the parameters; after 200 steps p(蓝) = 99.8% this site’s real model

ProblemHuman-labelled data is scarce and costly, which limits how much a model can learn.
Research · findingText carries its own answers: the next char is the label, no human needed. Shannon (1951) already measured how predictable English is by having people guess the next letter. GPT (2018) showed that pre-training like this, then fine-tuning, works clearly better.
DesignA Transformer with a causal mask predicts the next token on mass text, minimising cross-entropy.
Why it worksTo guess the next char well it must master grammar, facts and context; the material is almost endless, and bigger is better (see the “Scaling laws” card).
Scaling laws (Scaling Laws).
Estimates in advance how low the error can go when model, data and compute grow, and how best to split a fixed budget.

• Parameters N: how many numbers the model has
  • Data D: how many tokens training used
  • Compute C: the total computation, roughly C ≈ 6·N·D operations
  • Error L: cross-entropy on text never seen

1. The error follows a “power law” in N, D and C: close to a straight line on log–log axes; 10× bigger, the error falls by a roughly fixed ratio
  2. E.g. Chinchilla used 70 billion parameters and 1.4 trillion tokens, about the compute of the 280-billion-parameter Gopher, yet scored better on most tests

ProblemOne training run is very costly; you don’t know beforehand if it is “worth it”, or whether to spend on a bigger model or more data.
Research · findingKaplan et al. 2020 (OpenAI): the error falls as a power law in N, D and C across many orders of magnitude; details like depth and width matter relatively little; the conclusion then was to grow mainly the model as compute grows. Hoffmann et al. 2022 (DeepMind, Chinchilla) re-ran many experiments and found parameters and data should grow roughly in proportion, roughly about 20 tokens per parameter; many big models of the time had “many parameters, too little data”.
DesignTrain a batch of small models, fit the curve, then extrapolate to choose the big model’s size and data.
Why it worksIt is an empirical rule from experiments, not a theorem: accurate within the tested range, and the further you extrapolate, the more careful you must be.
Supervised fine-tuning, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT); with “instruction → answer” data it is also called instruction tuning.
Teaches a pre-trained model that can only “continue text” to follow instructions and answer properly, in format.

• Start: the pre-trained parameters
  • Demonstrations: human-written “instruction → good answer” examples
  • Chat template: special symbols tell “user” from “assistant”
  • Method: still guess the next char, usually counting the error on the answer only; smaller learning rate

1. A model that is only pre-trained may see “天空是什么颜色？” and go on with “草是什么颜色？” (What colour is grass?) — like continuing a worksheet example number
  2. Train on examples: “用户：天空是什么颜色？ 助手：通常是蓝色。” (User: what colour is the sky? Assistant: usually blue.)
  3. It learns to give an answer after “助手：” (Assistant:)

ProblemA pre-trained model imitates text on the web; it doesn’t answer questions by itself, and its format is messy.
Research · findingWei et al. 2021 (FLAN) rewrote many tasks as instructions for fine-tuning, and the model did clearly better zero-shot on unseen tasks; Ouyang et al. 2022 (InstructGPT) used demonstration answers written by labellers for SFT, as the first step of alignment.
DesignA small number of high-quality demonstrations, training on from the pre-trained parameters.
Why it worksMost knowledge is already learned in pre-training; fine-tuning mainly teaches “how to use it, how to answer”, so far fewer examples than pre-training material still work.
Alignment; a common method is RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.
Makes answers closer to what people want: more helpful, more honest, more harmless.

• Preference data: several answers to one question, ranked by people
  • Reward model: learns people’s preferences and scores answers
  • Reinforcement learning: (e.g. PPO): makes the model write high-scoring answers more often
  • Constraint: must not drift too far from the SFT model, to stop it “gaming the score”

1. Ask “天空是什么颜色？” A: Blue — air scatters more of the blue in sunlight. B: Don’t know, look it up.
  2. People pick A → the reward model learns to give A 8.2 points and B 1.5 example number
  3. Reinforcement learning makes the model write answers like A more often

ProblemA “good answer” is hard to write as a formula, and having people write every standard answer is costly; but people can easily say which of two answers is better.
Research · findingChristiano et al. 2017: people compared two pieces of behaviour, a reward function was learned, and with little human feedback it taught Atari games and simulated robot tasks. Ouyang et al. 2022 (InstructGPT) used three steps, SFT → reward model → PPO; labellers preferred the answers of the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT to those of the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3.
DesignCollect rankings → train a reward model → optimise with reinforcement learning; later came methods without reinforcement learning too, e.g. DPO (2023).
Why it worksComparing is easier than writing answers, and more consistent; the reward model spreads a few human judgements over a vast number of answers.

KC08.no: Changed in training, read in use
s: Model parameters (Parameters), also called weights (Weights).
Everything training learns is stored as these numbers; in use they are only read, never changed.

• Embedding table: dictionary size × d, one row per token
  • Attention weights: W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O in each layer
  • Feed-forward weights: two layers in each layer
  • Norm parameters: a few per layer
  • Output table: d × dictionary size, often shared with the embedding table in big models; this site’s small model does not share them

1. This demo: 14 chars (with END), d=16, 2 layers → 7406 numbers
  2. Rough count: each decoder block has about 12·d² numbers (attention 4d² + feed-forward 8d²)
  3. GPT-3: 96 layers, d=12288 → 12×96×12288² ≈ 174 billion, plus the embedding table ≈ 175 billion
  4. At 2 bytes per number, about 350 GB

ProblemLanguage has too many rules and exceptions to write by hand.
Research · findingThe universal approximation theorem (Cybenko 1989, Hornik et al. 1989): a large enough neural network can approximate very complex functions; gradient descent can tune these numbers automatically.
DesignA fixed structure + lots of trainable numbers: the structure decides “how to compute”, the numbers decide “what was learned”.
Why it worksTraining presses the patterns in the data into these numbers; scaling laws show that, with enough data, more parameters hold more patterns (see the “Scaling laws” card).
Inference / autoregressive generation (Autoregressive Generation).
Uses the trained parameters to continue your words one char at a time until it is done.

• Tokenize: text → numbers
  • Forward pass: the Transformer reads the parameters and computes odds
  • Pick: choose one by a rule (see the “Sampling and temperature” card)
  • Append: put it at the end
  • Stop: an end symbol or the length cap
  • KV cache: keeps results computed earlier

1. Round 1: “天空是什么颜色？” → 蓝
  2. Round 2: “…？蓝” → 色
  3. Round 3: “…蓝色” → 。
  4. Round 4 → the end symbol, stop
  5. Every round runs a forward pass; the KV cache means earlier chars are not recomputed, only the new one

ProblemThe model can only give the odds of the “next char” at a time, but we want a whole answer.
Research · findingThe chain rule of probability: a sentence’s odds = the product of each char’s conditional odds; pre-training learns exactly this target.
DesignGenerate char by char and feed each result back into the input, the same way as the causal mask in training.
Why it worksEach step is the model’s best skill, “guess the next char”. The cost: longer is slower; a wrong char can’t be taken back and affects what follows (see the “Hallucination” card).
Context window (Context Window), also called the context length, measured in tokens.
Sets how many tokens the model can “see” at once at most: your question, the earlier chat and the answer it has written so far all count.

• System prompt: instructions the developer put in first
  • Chat history: the earlier Q&A
  • This input: what you say this time
  • Answer so far: takes up room as it is written
  • Position encoding: decides how far positions can be numbered

1. Window = 20 tokens, 15 used → the answer can write at most 5 more example number
  2. When it is exceeded, the earliest content is cut off, or first compressed into a summary
  3. Real examples: GPT-2 is 1024, GPT-3 is 2048; many models today reach over a hundred thousand or more (roughly)

ProblemLonger windows cost more: in standard attention every char scores against all chars before it, so compute grows with the square of the length; and training only saw a certain length.
Research · findingTraining fixes a maximum length; later research improved position encoding (e.g. rotary position encoding RoPE, Su et al. 2021) and how attention is computed (e.g. FlashAttention, Dao et al. 2022), and windows kept growing.
DesignSet a cap; everything inside the window can “see” everything else.
Why it worksAny two chars inside the window connect directly; the model sees nothing outside it — so a long chat “forgets” its start, and summaries or retrieval must bring it back.
Sampling and temperature (Temperature); formula and full example: layer 4, the “Generation loop, sampling and temperature” card.
Decides which char to actually pick from the “next char” odds: safe, or varied.

• Greedy: always pick the most likely
  • Sample by odds: more likely, more often picked
  • Temperature T: divide the scores by T first, then turn them into odds
  • top-k: sample only among the top k candidates
  • top-p: sample only among the candidates up to a total of p

1. This site’s model before training: 草 22.9%, 什 14.8%, 绿 12.0% … 蓝 5.4% this site’s real model
  2. After training: 蓝 99.8%
  3. Greedy → “草” every time before training, “蓝” after
  4. Sample by odds → after training about 998 times “蓝” in 1000
  5. Lower temperature → more focused on the top char; higher → other chars get more chances

ProblemAlways picking the top: text gets repetitive and dull; fully random: it wanders off topic and odd chars pop up.
Research · findingFan et al. (2018) used top-k sampling for story generation; Holtzman et al. (2019) found that decoding for maximum probability tends to give repetitive, bland text, and proposed top-p (nucleus sampling).
DesignFirst use temperature to make the distribution “sharper” or “flatter”, then sample only among the leading candidates.
Why it worksLow temperature is steadier for factual Q&A; a slightly higher one is more inventive for writing and brainstorming.
Hallucination (Hallucination): fluent and real-sounding, but wrong or made up.
Understand why it happens, and learn to reduce it with prompts and retrieval.

• Causes (roughly): training aims to “sound right”, not “be right”; rare knowledge is blurry in the parameters; the training data itself is wrong or out of date; an early mistake gets carried on; sampling is random
  • Remedies: prompts, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), asking for sources, human checking

1. Ask a rare question the model never learned reliably → no candidate has high odds, but it must still pick a char and go on → it writes a “plausible-looking” answer
  2. RAG: first search a document store for relevant passages → put them in the context with the question → prompt “answer only from the material, cite the source; if it isn’t there, say you don’t know”

ProblemUsers think the model “knows”; it is really just continuing with the most likely text.
Research · finding(Roughly) the model’s parameters are a compression of the training data: frequent facts are held firmly, rare ones get mixed up; it has no “check the facts” step of its own.
DesignLewis et al. (2020) proposed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): retrieve documents first, then generate from them, so knowledge can be updated at any time; prompts ask for sources and allow “I don’t know”; alignment also rewards honest answers.
Why it worksWith the evidence right in the context, “writing from the material” is far more reliable than “writing from memory”; but it can’t be removed entirely, so important facts still need checking.
